You are sitting in a room that smells like rain and old paper. The window is open a crack, and the curtain lifts and falls like something breathing in its sleep. Outside, the world is doing its usual things—a dog barks somewhere, a car engine turns over, a child laughs at something only children understand. Inside, there is only you and the quiet hum of the small hours. This is the hour when thoughts stop being thoughts and become something else: a kind of weather.

I have been thinking about beginnings. How every story, every day, every life is just a series of small doors you didn't notice until you were already through them. The first sip of coffee in the morning is a door. The moment you decide to text someone you haven't spoken to in years—that's a door too. Sometimes you walk through and nothing changes. Sometimes you walk through and the whole house rearranges itself around you.

There is a particular loneliness to the hour before dawn, when the world is still wrapped in that blue-gray blanket of almost-light. It feels like the whole planet is holding its breath, waiting for something. Maybe waiting for you to decide what kind of day it will be. That's a lot of pressure to put on a single person, so mostly we just stumble to the kettle and let the day decide for us.

I've been thinking about memory, too. Not the big memories—birthdays, graduations, the day you first fell in love and the day you first realized love could hurt—but the small ones. The way sunlight falls on a particular kitchen table at exactly 4 p.m. The song that was playing when you learned to drive. The exact weight of a hand on your shoulder at a funeral. These are the bricks of who we are, and we don't even notice we're building with them.

The strange thing is that we remember moments, not durations. We remember the flash of lightning, not the whole storm. We remember the sentence, not the whole conversation. Somewhere inside us, time is being compressed into a series of photographs, and we spend our whole lives trying to arrange them into something that makes sense—a narrative, a meaning, a reason.

But maybe the meaning isn't in the arrangement. Maybe it's in the simple act of noticing. The way your mother's laugh sounded like a bell and a cough at the same time. The way your father always tilted his head when he was about to tell a joke. The way a stranger smiled at you on the bus and you never saw them again. Those are the moments that don't fit into any story, and yet they're the ones we carry longest.

I think about the people who are no longer here. Not in a sad way, but in the way you think about a book you loved as a child—you can't remember the plot, but you remember how it made you feel. The people we lose don't disappear. They just become part of the furniture of our minds. You'll catch yourself saying something in your father's voice. You'll hum a song your grandmother used to hum, and you won't even realize where it came from. They live in us like echoes in an empty room.

And I think about the future. The person I'll be in ten years. Will they recognize me? Will they remember this exact moment—sitting here, writing these words, the rain starting to fall on the roof—or will it be lost in the shuffle of a thousand other moments? I like to think they'll remember it. I like to think that some version of this moment will be one of the bricks in that wall of memory, and that this future version of me will look at it and understand something that I don't understand yet.

There's a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the bittersweet awareness of the impermanence of things. It's the feeling you get when you see cherry blossoms falling, beautiful precisely because they won't last. It's the ache in your chest when you watch a sunset and know you'll never see that exact one again. It's the knowledge that everything is borrowed, that all of this—the rain, the dog barking, the child laughing, the curtain breathing in its sleep—is on loan, and the loan comes due.

So maybe that's the answer. Maybe the point isn't to find meaning in the arrangement of moments, but to love them while they're happening. To be present for the small things. To notice the weight of your own hand on the table. To feel the texture of the page under your fingers. To listen to the rain like it's a song you've never heard before, because every rain is different, every rain is the last rain of its kind.

I don't know where this is going. I started with a room and a window and a curtain, and somehow I've ended up in philosophy, which is what always happens when you let your mind wander long enough. But that's the thing about writing—it's a door. You open it, and you don't know where you'll end up.

I think that's okay. I think that's the whole point.

The rain is still falling. The curtain is still breathing. And you are still here, reading these words, making your own meaning out of them. Which means you are a door too. And I'm glad you walked through.
